The Surah of the Pen (Sūrat al-Qalam) is Meccan (Makkiyya), except from verse seventeen to verse thirty-three, and from verse forty-eight to verse fifty, which are Medinan (Madaniyya). Its verses number fifty-two.

﴿Nūn﴾ is read with sukūn (silent vowel) because of pause (waqf). It is also read with kasra and with fatha, due to the meeting of two silent letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The fatha may be explained by an elided particle of oath in the place of the genitive, as in their saying: Allāhi la-af'alanna (by God, I will surely do it), with the genitive. It may also be an accusative governed by an implied verb, "udhkur" (mention), not as a fatha, as has been explained at the opening of Sūrat al-Baqara. The non-declension (imtināʿ al-ṣarf) is due to definiteness and femininity, on the basis that it is a proper name for the surah. Then, if it is taken as the name of the letter, listed in the manner of enumeration for the challenge (taḥaddī), by one of the two methods mentioned in its place; or as the name of the surah, in the accusative in the manner mentioned; or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, then the wāw in His saying, ﴿wal-qalam﴾ (and by the pen), is for oath. If it is taken as the thing sworn by, then the wāw is for coordination with it. In any case, if by it is meant the pen of the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ) and the noble scribes, then its deserving of glorification by swearing by it is evident. If by it is meant the genus (of pens), then the deserving of what is in people's hands for this is due to the abundance of its benefits. Even if it had no merit other than being an instrument for writing down the books of God, Mighty and Majestic, it would suffice as a virtue requiring its glorification. It is also read with idghām (assimilation) of the nūn into the wāw.

﴿And what they inscribe﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the pen, indicated by mentioning it. It was said: it refers to the pen, on the understanding that what is meant is its people, as if it were said: "and the people of the pen and what they write," if "mā" is a relative pronoun (meaning "what"), or "and their writing," if it is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya). It was said: it refers to the pen itself, by attributing the verb to the instrument and treating it as rational, since it stands in their place. It was said: what is meant by the pen is specifically what wrote on the Tablet, and the plural is for glorification. His saying, Exalted is He:

Verse 2: "You are not, by the blessing of your Lord, a madman."

The answer to the oath. The preposition bi- (with/by) is connected to an implied verb, which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in its predicate. The element governing it is the sense of negation, as if it were said: "You are free of madness, joined with the blessing of God, which is prophethood and general leadership." The mention of the attribute of Lordship (rububiyyah), which indicates conveying (the message) to the heights of perfection, together with its addition to his pronoun ﷺ, is for his honour (ﷺ), and to announce that He, exalted is He, completes His blessing upon him and brings him from loftiness to a degree beyond which there is no further degree. The intent is to declare him (ﷺ) free of what they used to attribute to him (ﷺ) of madness, out of envy, enmity and obstinacy, even though they were certain that he (ﷺ) was at the utmost extreme of remoteness and the furthest limit of soundness of intellect and steadiness of judgement.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 68, verse 3:

﴿And indeed for you﴾ in return for your enduring the various kinds of hardship from them, and your bearing the burdens of the Message, ﴿is a reward﴾, a great recompense whose worth cannot be measured, ﴿never-ending﴾ despite its greatness, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a gift not cut off﴾ (Qur'an 11:108). Or it means "not taken back from you by people": it is His gift, exalted is He, without any intermediary.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 4:

﴿And indeed you are of a magnificent character.﴾ No one among the creation can attain its reach (sha'w), and therefore he bears from them what hardly any human being could bear. "'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was asked about his character (ﷺ), and she said: 'His character was the Qur'an. Do you not recite the Qur'an? "Successful indeed are the believers."'" And the two clauses are conjoined to the answer of the oath.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 5:

﴿So you will see, and they will see.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "You will know and they will know on the Day of Resurrection, when the truth is distinguished from falsehood." It was also said: "You will see and they will see in this world, through the manifestation of the outcome of your affair with the victory of Islam, your dominion over them through killing and plunder, and your becoming awe-inspiring and held in great esteem in the hearts of the worlds, and their being humiliated and abased." Muqatil said: "This is a threat of the punishment of the Day of Badr."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 6:

﴿Which of you is the afflicted one﴾. That is: which of you is the one who has been afflicted with madness? The bā' is extra (zā'idah), or the sense is: "With which of you is the madness," on the basis that "al-maftūn" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like "al-ma'qūl" and "al-majlūd." Or the sense is: "Which of the two groups among you is the madman: the group of believers, or the group of disbelievers?" That is: in which of the two is found the one who deserves this name. This is a veiled reference (ta'ridh) to Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and their like, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent﴾ [al-Qamar 54:26]; and His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His path.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for what is indicated by what precedes it, namely the manifest evidence of their madness, to such an extent that it is hidden from no one, and a confirmation of the promise and threat contained therein. That is: He is most knowing of who has strayed from His path, exalted is He, which leads to the happiness of both abodes, and has wandered in the bewilderment of misguidance, heading toward what leads to everlasting wretchedness. This is the madman who cannot distinguish between benefit and harm, rather he considers harm to be benefit and prefers it, and considers benefit to be harm and abandons it. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ to His path, those who attain every desired goal and are saved from every feared thing, the sound-minded who have the upper hand, so that He recompenses each of the two groups according to what it deserves of punishment and reward. The repetition of "He is most knowing" is for the sake of added emphasis. And the fa' in His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 8:

﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ The particle (fa) here indicates that the prohibition is consequent upon what precedes it, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) guidance and their misguidance, or upon the whole of what has been detailed from the beginning of the surah. This is an incitement and a spurring on to steadfastness in opposing them; that is: persist in what you are upon, namely not obeying them, and be firm in that. Or it is a prohibition against flattering them and accommodating them by displaying what is contrary to what is in his (ﷺ) heart, in order to win over their hearts, not a prohibition against obeying them, as indicated by the words of the Exalted:

The commentary on ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾, the clause ﴿وَدُّوا لَوْ تُدْهِنُ﴾, begins: it is a reason (ta'līl) for the prohibition or for the cessation (of obedience) implied in it. He expressed the prohibition through the notion of obedience (al-ṭā'a) for the sake of emphasis in restraining and deterring (the Prophet). That is, they wish that you would be soft toward them and tolerate them in some matters, ﴿so they would compromise﴾. That is, ﴿فَيُدْهِنُونَ﴾ means: they would then compromise, or they are now compromising out of hope for your compromise. It has also been said that it is conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to "tudhin" (تُدْهِنُ) and falls within the scope of "law" (لَوْ), and the meaning is: they wish that, following your compromise, they would compromise. What rules this out is that what comes afterward, their initiating compromise (bid'uhum bil-idhān) over their own compromise, is a certain matter (amr muḥaqqaq), which is not suitable to include under the scope of wishing (tamannī).

In any case, what is considered on their side is the true reality of compromise (ḥaqīqat al-idhān), which is the display of softness while concealing its opposite. As for his side (ﷺ), what is considered in relation to their desire is only the display of softness, and the concealing of its opposite is not within the scope of consideration; rather, they are in the utmost of aversion to him, and his consideration relates only to the display of softness.

Some copies of the Qur'an read ﴿فَيُدْهِنُوا﴾ (fa-yudhinū), in which case it is the answer to the wish (tamannī, optative) understood from "waddū" (وَدُّوا), or what follows it is a narration of their desire. It has also been said that it is conjoined to "tudhin" on the basis that "law" (لَوْ) functions as "an" (أنْ, the subjunctive particle), so it has no answer (jawāb). From it and what follows it a verbal noun (maṣdar) is formed, which serves as the object of "waddū", as if it were said: they wish that you would compromise and they would compromise. It has also been said that "law" retains its literal meaning and its answer is omitted, as is the object of "waddū", meaning: they wish for your compromise; if you compromised and they compromised, they would be delighted by that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 10:

﴿And do not obey every habitual swearer⁠—﴾ the one who swears much, whether in truth or in falsehood. The mention of this attribute before the other attributes that restrain one from obedience is because it is more fitting to deter (one from obeying him), ﴿contemptible﴾, of base opinion and planning.

Translation:

﴿Backbiter﴾, a defamer and slanderer, ﴿going about with malicious gossip﴾, one who stirs up strife, who carries talk from one people to another in order to make mischief and cause corruption among them. For al-namim and al-namimah both mean tattling (al-si'ayah).

﴿Mannāʿin lil-khayr﴾ means: niggardly, or one who withholds people from the good, which is faith, obedience, and spending (in charity). ﴿Muʿtadin﴾ means: one who exceeds the bounds in wrongdoing. ﴿Athīm﴾ means: one who commits many sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 13:

﴿Ghulla﴾ (ʿutull) – harsh, coarse, rough; from ʿatalahu, meaning he drove him forcefully and roughly. ﴿After that﴾ – after what has been enumerated of his faults. ﴿Zanim﴾ (zanīm) – an illegitimate claimant of lineage (daʿī); it is derived from al-zanama, which is a piece of skin from the throat of a she-goat that is cut off and left hanging down from its throat. In His saying, Exalted is He, "after that," there is an indication that his illegitimate claim of lineage is the worst of his defects and the most ugly of his vices. It has been said: he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, for he was an illegitimate claimant of lineage among the Quraysh, not being of their stock; al-Mughira claimed him after he had been eighteen years from his birth. It has also been said: he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose origin is from Thaqif, and whose affiliation is among Zuhra.

(p-14) ﴿Because he possesses wealth and sons﴾ is connected to His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And do not obey﴾, meaning: do not obey one whose faults are these, because he is wealthy and relies upon his sons. And His, exalted be He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 15:

﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) functioning as a rationale (ta'lil) for the prohibition. It has also been said that it is connected to what the conditional sentence implies of denial (al-juhud), namely the act of rejection (al-takdhib), rather than to the apodosis (jawab al-shart), because what follows the conditional particle does not govern what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "Because he is relying on wealth and sons, he denied Our verses." In this there is a flaw, since it makes the basis of his denial his being possessed of wealth and sons, without any of his other vile qualities having a share in that.

It was also read as "a'an kana" (أأنْ كانَ), meaning: "Because he possesses wealth, does he deny them?" or "Will you obey him because he possesses wealth?" It was read as "in kana" with a kasra (إنْ كانَ بِالكَسْرِ), and the conditional is then addressed to the listener (al-mukhatab), meaning: Do not obey every oath-taker (haffaf) who stipulates his ease (yasar) for himself, because obeying a disbeliever on account of his wealth is equivalent to making his wealth a condition for obedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 16:

﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ By branding him on the most honorable part of his face, for the utmost degradation and humiliation of him. It was said: a wound struck the nose of al-Walid on the day of Badr and its mark remained. It was also said that its meaning is: We will mark him on the Day of Resurrection with a disfiguring sign by which he will be distinguished from the rest of the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, We tested them﴾, that is, the people of Makkah, with drought, through the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿as We tested the companions of the garden﴾. They were a people from among the People of the Prayer (ahl al-salat). This garden belonged to their father, two farsakhs (a unit of distance) short of Sana'a. He would take from it the provision of a year and give the remainder in charity. He used to call out to the poor at the time of harvesting (al-siram) and would leave for them what the sickle missed, what was at the bottom of the heaps of grain, what the picking of grapes missed, and what remained on the cloth spread beneath the palm tree when it was cut down. A great deal would thus accumulate for them. When their father died, his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will be too hard for us." So they swore among themselves, and that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when they swore that they would surely harvest it in the morning﴾, that is, that they would cut it off, entering upon the morning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 18:

﴿And they did not make exception⦆ That is: they did not say, "If Allah wills" (in shā' Allāh). Its being called istithnā' (exception) even though it is a condition (sharṭ) is because its import is the import of istithnā', for your saying, "I will certainly go out, if Allah wills," and "I will not go out except that Allah wills," have one meaning. Or it means: "and they did not set aside the share of the poor," as their father used to do. The sentence is a new, independent clause (mustaʼnafah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 19:

﴿So there passed over it﴾, that is, over the garden, ﴿a visitation﴾, a calamity that passed over it. It is also read as (طَيْفٌ, *ṭayf*), ﴿from your Lord﴾, a beginning from His direction, exalted is He, ﴿while they were asleep﴾, heedless of what the decrees had brought about.

(p-15) ﴿So it became like a Ṣarīm﴾ — like a garden whose fruit had been cut off, such that nothing of it remained; ṣarīm here is on the pattern fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl (cut off). It was also said: like the night, i.e., it was burned and blackened. And it was said: like the day, i.e., it dried up and turned white. Each of these was called ṣarīm because each of them is cut off from its companion. And it was said: al-ṣarīm means the sand dunes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 21:

﴿Then they called out to one another﴾, that is, some of them called to others, ﴿at morning-time﴾, entering into the morning.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 68, verse 22:

﴿That go forth early⁠﴾ — i.e., go forth early, [taking "an" (that) as] explanatory (mufassira), or [taking it as] with "an" (that) being verbal (masdariyya), i.e., "go out in the morning" (ghadwa). ﴿To your tilth⁠﴾ — your orchard and your plantation. The verb ghadw (going out in the morning) is followed by "ʿalā" (upon/to) because it is made to imply the sense of coming upon (al-iqbal) or taking control of (al-istila'). ﴿If you are determined to cut [the fruit]⁠﴾ — intending to harvest (li-l-sarm).

﴿So they set off, speaking to one another in low voices.﴾ That is, they consulted among themselves in a whispered manner. The roots خفي (kh-f-y), خفت (kh-f-t) and خفد (kh-f-d) all carry the sense of concealing, and from the last comes الخُفْدود (al-khufdud), the word for the bat (khuffash).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 24:

﴿That no poor man shall enter it (the Garden) today upon you﴾. "That" (an, mufassira) is explanatory, interpreting the sense of speech contained in "they whispered (yatakhafatun)". It is also read without it (an), with the verb of saying implied. The purpose of the prohibition addressed to the poor man against entering is to emphasize the strictness of the prohibition against enabling him to enter, like their saying: "Let me not see you here."

ﷻ﴿وَغَدَوْا عَلى حَرْدٍ قادِرِينَ﴾ (And they set out early, resolved in their intent (ḥard), confident of their power.) Namely: "upon distress (nakad) and nothing else," from jāradat al-sanah (the year was barren), when there was no rain, and ḥāradat al-ibil (the she-camels withheld their milk), when they withheld their milk. The meaning is that they intended to distress the poor and deprive them, while they were able to benefit them. So they set out in a state in which they could only attain distress and deprivation, because they sought to deprive the poor and thus hastened upon themselves deprivation and poverty. Or: "and they set out upon the withholding of their garden and the loss of its good, able to ..." instead of being able to obtain its good and its benefits; that is, they set out having obtained distress and deprivation instead of being able to benefit. It was also said: al-ḥard means al-ḥard (the same word, a form read as such), and it has been recited thus; that is, they were only able to be enraged at one another, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَتَلاوَمُونَ﴾ (they blame one another). It was also said: al-ḥard means intention and haste; that is, they set out intending their garden swiftly, confident in themselves of harvesting it. It was also said: it is a proper name for the garden.
﴿When they saw it, they said﴾ at the very first sight of it, ﴿"Indeed, we have gone astray"﴾, meaning: "We have lost the way to our garden, and this is not it."

(p-16) ﴿Nay, we are deprived﴾. They said this after they had reflected and come to understand the reality of the matter, turning away from their former statement. That is: "We are not astray; rather, we are deprived (maḥrūmūn), we have been deprived of its good through our own offense against ourselves."

﴿The most moderate of them said﴾, that is, in opinion or in age: ﴿Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify [God]?"﴾ That is, "Why do you not remember God, the Exalted, and turn back to Him in repentance from the wickedness of your intention?" He had told them, when they resolved upon that, "Remember God and repent to Him immediately from this wicked resolve, and hasten to put an end to its evil before the punishment befalls." But they disobeyed him, so he rebuked them, as indicated by the words of God, the Exalted:

They said, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed we were wrongdoers." It is also said that what is meant by the tasbih (glorification of God) is the istithna' (exception, i.e., saying "if God wills"), since both share in magnifying Him. Or it is a declaration of His transcendence, exalted is He, above anything occurring in His dominion that He does not will.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 30:

﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ That is: some of them blamed others, for among them were those who had proposed this plan, and among them were those who approved of it, and among them were those who kept silent, content with it, and among them were those who disapproved of it.
"They said, 'O woe to us! Indeed we were transgressors,'" meaning: exceeding the limits of Allah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 32:

﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it.﴾ It is also read with shaddah (yubaddilanā), meaning: He will give us in its place something better, through the blessing of repentance and acknowledgment of the sin. ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are turning eagerly.﴾ That is, hoping for pardon and seeking good. The "ilā" (to) here indicates the endpoint of the desire, or because it implies the meaning of returning. From Mujahid: they repented, so they were given in exchange something better than it. It is also narrated that they made a pact among themselves and said: "If Allah gives us in exchange something better than it, we will surely do as our father did," so they called upon Allah, the Exalted, and humbled themselves before Him, and Allah, the Exalted, gave them in exchange, from that very night, something better than it. They said: Allah, the Exalted, commanded Jibril, peace be upon him, to uproot that burnt garden and place it at the edge of the land of Sham, and to take from Sham a garden and place it in its stead. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When the people became sincere and Allah knew their truthfulness, He gave them a garden called al-Hayawan, in which there are grapes, of which a mule could carry a single cluster. Abu Khalid al-Yamani said: I entered that garden and saw that each of its clusters was like a standing black man. Qatadah was asked about the people of the garden: Are they from the people of Paradise or from the people of the Fire? He said: "You have burdened me with a great effort." From al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: as for the statement of the companions of the garden, ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are turning eagerly,﴾ he said: "I do not know whether that was faith on their part, or whether it was in the manner of the polytheists when hardship afflicts them; so he withheld judgment regarding their matter." Most scholars hold that they repented and were sincere, as related by al-Qushayri.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 33:

(p-17) ﴿Such is the punishment﴾ is a sentence consisting of a subject (mubtada') and a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) for the purpose of restriction (qasr). The alif and lam (in al-'adhab) are for previous reference (al-'ahd), meaning: like that with which We tested the people of Makkah and the people of the garden, is the punishment of this world.

﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾, more magnificent and more severe, ﴿if only they knew﴾ that it is greater, they would have guarded against what leads them to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, for the God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾ i.e., from disbelief and sins ﴿with their Lord﴾ i.e., in the Hereafter, or in the proximity of the holy presence ﴿are gardens of bliss﴾, gardens in which there is nothing but pure enjoyment, free from any admixture of what would spoil it of turbidities and the fear of its ending, as is the case with the bliss of this world. And His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 35:

﴿Shall We then make the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ This is an affirmation of what precedes it, namely the triumph of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) with the Gardens of Bliss, and a refutation of what the disbelievers (al-kafarah) say when they hear the discourse about the Hereafter. As for what God promised the Muslims therein, they would say: "If it is true that we will be resurrected, as Muhammad and those with him claim, then our state and their state will be nothing but like what it is in this world; and if not, they would not have any advantage over us, nor would they surpass us. At most, their situation would be that they equal us." The hamza (hamzah) is for denial (li-l-inkar), and the fa' (fa') is for coordination (li-l-atf) with an implied clause required by the context, meaning: "Shall We deviate in judgment, so that We make the Muslims like the disbelievers?" Then, by way of iltifat (iltifat, a shift in grammatical person), it was said to them, to emphasize and intensify the refutation.

﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ This expresses wonder at their judgment and the consideration of it as far-fetched, and it signifies that such a judgment does not come from any rational person.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 37:

﴿Or do you have a Book﴾ sent down from the heaven ﴿in which you study﴾, i.e., you read.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, for you therein is whatever you choose.﴾ That is: whatever you select (takhayyarun) and desire (tashtahunahu). Its original form is "inna lakum" with the letter alif pointed with a fatha (anna lakum), because it is something studied (madrus, i.e., something one has learned from a book); but when the lam was brought in, the alif was given a kasra. It is also permissible that it be a quotation of what is studied (hikayah li-l-madrus), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾. And the meaning of takhayyur al-shay' and ikhtiyaruhu (choosing something) is: taking its best (khayrihi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 39:

﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us﴾, that is: firm covenants confirmed by oaths, ﴿reaching (bāligha)﴾, meaning extremely emphatic in their confirmation. It has also been read in the accusative (bāligatan) as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), the governing element in it being one of the two adverbial phrases. ﴿Until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to the implied element in "lakum" (for you), meaning: they remain valid for you until the Day of Resurrection, and We will not depart from their obligation until We judge you on that Day and give you what you decide upon. Alternatively, "bāligha" is read as an adjective of "ayman" (oaths), meaning: oaths that reach that day and end at it, complete, such that no oath of them has been nullified. ﴿Indeed, for you is what you judge﴾ is the answer of the oath, because the meaning of "Or do you have oaths binding upon Us" is: "Or have We sworn to you?" (p-18)

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 40:

﴿Ask them﴾ is a shift (talwin) in the mode of address, turning the discourse toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by removing them from the rank of being addressed directly. That is: ask them, rebuking them, ﴿which of them stands surety for that﴾ judgment, which lies outside the bounds of reason? ﴿Stands surety (za'im)﴾ means: one who is standing forward to vouch for its soundness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 41:

﴿Or do they have associates?﴾ who share with them in this claim and follow their path.

﴿Then let them bring their associates, if they are truthful﴾ in their claim; for at least it would be imitation (taqlid, following others without evidence). In these noble verses He has alerted that they have nothing that could be imagined as something to cling to, not even imitation, which does not bring success to whoever clings to its tail. It was also said that the meaning is: Or do they have associates whom they make like the Muslims in the Hereafter?

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 42:

﴿On the Day when a shin will be laid bare﴾. That is: on the day when the matter becomes severe and the affair grows dire. The "laying bare of the shin" is a metaphor for this, and its origin is the hitching up of skirts by women (mukhaddarat) to their shins when fleeing. Hatim said:

"A man of war: if war bites him, he bites back; and if war hitches up its shin, he hitches up too."

It is also said: the shin (saq) of a thing is its root upon which its stability rests, like the trunk of a tree or the shin of a person. That is: on the day when the root of the matter is laid bare, the realities and origins of affairs become manifest, so that they become plain to sight. Its indefiniteness (tankir) is for terrifying (li-l-tahwil) or for magnifying (li-l-ta'zim). It was also read as (tukshifu) with the ta' in the active and passive forms, the verb being attributed to the Hour or to the situation; and it was read as (nukshifu) with the nun, and as (tuksafu) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the shin, from ukshifa al-amr, meaning it entered into being revealed. The adverbial object (zarf) is governed by "falya'tu" (then let them come), or by a hidden verb placed before it, meaning: remember the day of..., etc.; or placed after it, meaning: on the day when a shin will be laid bare..., etc. There will occur on that day of terrors and great conditions what description cannot reach.

﴿And they will be summoned to prostrate﴾, as a rebuke and reproach for their having abandoned it in the world, and as a cause of regret for their neglect in that matter.

﴿But they will not be able﴾, because the capacity for it has gone. In this there is an indication that they intend to prostrate, yet it does not come about for them. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Their backbones will be made rigid," meaning they are returned as bones without joints, not bending at bowing or prostration. In a hadith: "and their backbones will remain one single layer," meaning one single vertebra.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 43:

﴿Their eyes downcast﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the nominative pronoun in "they are called" (yuds'awn), on the basis that "their eyes" is raised by it as the agent (fā'il). The attribution of humility (khushū') to the eyes is because its effect becomes apparent in them.

﴿Shall cover them﴾ means: shall reach them and overwhelm them.

﴿Humiliation﴾ means: intense.

﴿And they used to be called to prostration﴾ in the world; the explicit mention in place of the pronoun is for added emphasis (taqrīr), or because what is meant by it is prayer (al-ṣalāh), or what is in it of prostration (al-sujūd), and the calling is the calling of obligation (da'wat al-taklīf).

﴿While they were sound﴾ means: fully able to do it in the most complete way; that is, they would not respond to it and would refuse it. Its mention was omitted out of confidence in its being evident.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 44:

﴿So leave Me alone with those who deny this discourse.﴾ That is: entrust their affair to Me, for I will suffice you in their matter. That is, what is sufficient for you in striking them and taking vengeance upon them is that you entrust their affair to Me and leave between Me and them; for I am Knowing of what punishment they deserve and Capable of inflicting it upon them. The "fa'" (the fa' of consequence) is for the ordering of the command upon what precedes it of their states that have been related, that is: and since their condition in the Hereafter is such, then leave Me alone with those who deny this Qur'an, and rely upon Me for taking vengeance upon them. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿We shall draw them on step by step﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the manner of the punishment that is derived in summary from the preceding command. The pronoun refers to "man" (those), and the plural is in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular in "yukadhdhibu" (denies) is in consideration of its wording. That is: We shall lead them down to the punishment degree by degree, by bestowing favour, perpetuating health and increasing blessing.

﴿From where they do not know﴾: that it is istidraj (gradual drawing-on), which is bestowing favour upon them. Rather, they suppose that it is preference given to them and favouring them over the believers, although it is in fact a cause of their destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 45:

﴿And I give them respite﴾. I grant them time, so that they may increase in sin, while they suppose that this is for the sake of good being intended for them.

﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾. It cannot be detected, nor can it be repelled by anything; and calling it "plan" (kayd) is because it is in the form of a plan.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 46:

﴿Or do you ask them for a reward?﴾ For conveying and guiding.

﴿A reward﴾ worldly.

﴿So they﴾ because of that.

﴿Are burdened with debt﴾ i.e., a financial penalty.

﴿Burdened﴾ made to bear a heavy load, so they turn away from you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 47:

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write (it) down?﴾ That is: the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or the hidden things (al-mughayyabat). ﴿So they write from it what they judge by, and dispense with your knowledge through it.﴾

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 48:**

﴿So be patient with the decree of your Lord﴾, that is, with His granting them respite and the delay of your victory over them.

﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾, that is, Yunus (peace be upon him).

﴿When he called out﴾ from within the belly of the fish.

﴿while he was ˹inwardly˺ distressed﴾: filled with rage. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject of "called out," and the prohibition revolves around it, not around the calling out itself, for calling out is a commendable act. For this reason the one called upon is not mentioned. "Idh" (when) is governed by an omitted noun it is attached to, meaning: "Let your condition not be like his condition at the time of his calling out," that is: let there not be found in you what was found in him of impatience and displeasure, lest you be tested with his affliction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 49:

﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him﴾. It is also read as "mercy" (raḥmah), and this is His granting him success in repentance and accepting it from him. The verb is masculine in form (taddārakahu) because the intervening pronoun separates it from the subject, which is good usage. It is also read as "taddārakat-hu" and "tadārakahu", meaning "tatadārakahu" (it would have overtaken him), in the narrative of a past state, in the sense of "had it not been that it was being said: tatadārakuhu" (it would overtake him).

﴿He would have been cast out onto the open plain﴾, onto bare land empty of trees.

﴿while he was blameworthy﴾, reprehensible and expelled from mercy and honour. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "nubidha" (was cast out), and the answer to "lawlā" (had it not been) depends on it, because it is the negated element, not the casting out onto the open plain, as was mentioned in the first circumstance. The conditional sentence is a resumptive clause coming to explain that what is forbidden is a dreaded matter entailing a harmful consequence. As for His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 50:

﴿So his Lord chose him⁠﴾ is conjoined to something implied, meaning: a blessing from his Lord overtook him, and He chose him by restoring revelation to him and sending him to (p-20) a hundred thousand or more. It is also said: He made him a prophet (istanba'ahu), if it is sound that he was not a prophet before this incident.

﴿And He made him among the righteous⁠﴾ means among those perfect in righteousness, by protecting him from doing an act whose abandonment would be better. It is narrated that it was revealed at Uhud when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to invoke curses upon the Muslims who had fled. It is also said: it was when he wanted to invoke curses upon the tribe of Thaqif.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 68, verse 51:

﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes﴾. It is read (also): (la-yazlaqūnaka) with a fatḥah on the yā', from zalaqahu, meaning: azlaqahu (made him slip), and (yuzhiqūnaka) (they would make you perish). The "in" here is the light (mukhaffafah) form (of inna), the lām being its indicator, and the meaning is: because of the intensity of their enmity towards you, they look at you sidelong (shazran), such that they almost make your foot slip so that they can strike you down, from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocked me down," i.e., if his glance were able to bring about the knocking down, he would have done it. Or it means that they would almost afflict you with the evil eye (al-'ayn), since it has been related that among the Banu Asad there were people with the evil eye, and some of them wanted to afflict the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so this verse was revealed. In a hadith: "Indeed the evil eye brings a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot." Perhaps this is among the properties of certain souls. And from al-Hasan: the remedy for being afflicted by the evil eye is that you recite this verse.

﴿When they heard the Reminder﴾, i.e., at the time of their hearing the Qur'an, with "lamma" being a temporal adverb governed by "yuzliqūnaka", and this is due to the intensity of their hatred and envy upon hearing it.

﴿And they say﴾ out of the utmost of their bewilderment regarding his matter, peace and blessings be upon him, and the extreme of their ignorance of the wondrous wisdoms and marvellous sciences within the folds of the Qur'an, which are hidden from minds immersed in the rulings of natures, and to repel people from him.

﴿Indeed he is surely a madman﴾. And since the basis of their false judgement was what they heard from him, peace and blessings be upon him, this was refuted by demonstrating the exaltedness of his station and the brightness of his proof, so it was said:

﴿And it is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾, being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "they say" (yaqūlūn). It serves to emphasize the complete falsehood of their statement and to express astonishment at the audacity of the listeners in uttering such a grave claim. That is: they say this while the reality is that it is a reminder to the worlds, meaning an admonition and an explanation of everything they need in matters of their religion. How, then, could it be attributed to one upon whom it was revealed, who is fully aware of its secrets and comprehensively knows all its realities, as they claimed? It has also been said that its meaning is honor and excellence, based on the words of God Most High: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that his being an admonisher and an honor to the worlds is beyond doubt. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Qalam, God will grant him the reward of those whose character God has made beautiful."
